0.long_answer: Albers-Schönberg disease is the benign, autosomal-dominant form of osteopetrosis (marble-bone disease). Radiographically the skeleton shows uniformly dense, ‘bone-within-bone’ or ‘sandwich vertebra’ appearances. Clinically, bones are abnormally hard yet brittle, predisposing to pathological fractures; some patients develop cranial-nerve compression, mild anaemia, or osteomyelitis of the mandible, but overall the course is relatively mild compared with the malignant infantile form.

Marshall-Smith syndrome is an ultra-rare NFIX-related genetic disorder whose hallmark radiographic feature is abnormal endochondral (often mis-stated as “endocrine”) ossification leading to markedly accelerated skeletal maturation (advanced bone age). Patients show precocious appearance of ossification centers in the hands, feet and other bones, confirming the diagnosis.

There are several well-characterised, Mendelian disorders in which the cardinal findings are markedly small, malformed eyes (microphthalmia/anophthalmia with structural disorganisation) together with upper- and/or lower-limb malformations. Examples include:
• Lenz microphthalmia syndrome (X-linked; pathogenic variants in BCOR) – severe bilateral microphthalmia/anophthalmia, radial ray defects, syndactyly, phalangeal hypoplasia.
• Ocular-limb dysplasia due to SMOC1 mutations (MCOPS9) – microphthalmia with coloboma plus post-axial or meso-axial polydactyly, syndactyly, and limb reduction defects.
• Fraser syndrome (FRAS1, FREM2, GRIP1) – cryptophthalmos or severe microphthalmia together with syndactyly, limb reduction and digital anomalies.
• SOX2-related anophthalmia syndrome – bilateral anophthalmia/microphthalmia often accompanied by radial aplasia or 2–3 toe syndactyly.
• Cornelia de Lange syndrome (NIPBL, SMC1A, etc.) – small structurally abnormal eyes with characteristic upper-limb reduction defects.
These conditions are widely documented in the clinical-genetics literature and are accepted by consensus as causes of the combined eye-and-limb malformation phenotype. Hence, the statement that there are known genetic conditions associating unusually small, structurally disorganised eyes with limb anomalies is correct.

0.long_answer: When the adrenal glands are surgically removed (bilateral adrenalectomy), circulating cortisol and other adrenal steroids fall abruptly. The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis operates by negative feedback: cortisol normally suppresses both corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) from the hypothalamus and adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) from the anterior pituitary. With cortisol absent, this feedback inhibition is lost. As a result, CRH secretion rises, which drives a marked increase in ACTH release. The elevated ACTH represents the body’s attempt to stimulate the missing adrenal cortex to restore glucocorticoid levels; although no adrenal tissue is present to respond, the pituitary continues to secrete large amounts of ACTH. Persistently high ACTH can produce secondary effects such as skin hyperpigmentation (via melanocortin receptor activation) and hypertrophy of any residual or ectopic adrenal tissue. Thus, increased ACTH secretion is a key compensatory response after adrenal gland removal.

1.long_answer: Paramyotonia congenita is an autosomal-dominant disorder of skeletal-muscle excitability produced by gain-of-function mutations in the SCN4A gene that encodes the Nav1.4 voltage-gated sodium channel. Its hallmark is myotonia (delayed relaxation) that is triggered and WORSENS with repeated muscle contractions or exposure to cold—termed paradoxical myotonia, because, unlike classic myotonia, it does not warm-up but instead intensifies. After prolonged activity, patients can develop transient flaccid weakness. Thus the syndrome is characterized by cold- and exercise-induced myotonia that paradoxically aggravates with continued effort and may be followed by episodic weakness.

Aprataxin is indeed directly involved in DNA repair. It works in the single-strand break repair (SSBR) pathway, where failed ligation events can leave an abnormal 5′-adenylated DNA terminus (a 5′-AMP cap). Aprataxin has a DNA 5′-AMP phosphatase activity that removes this adenylate group, restoring a normal 5′-phosphate end so that DNA ligase can complete the repair. Through its interaction with XRCC1-DNA ligase IIIα complexes, aprataxin prevents the accumulation of toxic abortive ligation intermediates and thereby maintains genome stability. Loss of aprataxin activity (e.g., in APTX-mutated ataxia-oculomotor apraxia 1) leads to defective SSBR and genomic instability, confirming its critical role in DNA repair.

Yes. A wide range of pathogenic mutations that affect the proton-pumping complexes of the oxidative-phosphorylation (OXPHOS) chain are well documented to compromise formation of the electrochemical proton gradient (Δp) across the inner mitochondrial membrane. Examples include:

1. Complex I (NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase) – Proton pump
   • mtDNA‐encoded subunits ND1, ND2, ND3, ND4, ND5, ND6.  Classic pathogenic point mutations such as m.3460G>A (ND1), m.11778G>A (ND4) and m.14484T>C (ND6) found in Leber hereditary optic neuropathy impair electron transfer and proton extrusion, diminishing the gradient.

2. Complex III (cytochrome bc1) – Contributes to proton translocation by the Q-cycle
   • MT-CYB mutations (e.g., m.15257G>A or large deletions) reduce proton pumping efficiency.

3. Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) – Terminal proton pump
   • mtDNA mutations in COI, COII or COIII, and nuclear mutations such as in SURF1, SCO1/2, or COX10 genes, cause COX deficiency that directly lowers proton motive force.

4. Complex V (ATP synthase/F0F1) – Uses the gradient but the F0 sector also conducts protons; certain mutations cause proton leak
   • The well-studied m.8993T>G or m.8993T>C mutation in MT-ATP6 (NARP/Leigh syndrome) alters the proton channel of the F0 subunit, leading to dissipation of the gradient.

5. Assembly‐factor genes (e.g., NDUFAF2 for complex I, SURF1 for complex IV, TMEM70 for complex V) – Mutations block assembly of the proton pumps, indirectly preventing a normal Δp from forming.

Because these mutations disrupt either the structure, function, or assembly of the respiratory complexes that extrude protons, they are unequivocally accepted by the biomedical community as causes of impaired proton‐gradient generation.

Multiple independent genetic studies and reviews have confirmed CTSC as the sole gene whose mutations cause classic PLS, establishing this association as part of current biomedical consensus.

A variety of pharmacologic agents are well-established for reducing hyperglycaemia and thereby relieving the cardinal manifestations of diabetes mellitus (polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, fatigue, hyperglycaemia-related complications). Agents with documented efficacy include:
• Insulin preparations (rapid-, short-, intermediate- and long-acting) – cornerstone therapy for type 1 diabetes and advanced type 2 diabetes; promptly lowers plasma glucose and reverses acute symptoms.
• Metformin (a biguanide) – first-line oral therapy in type 2 diabetes; improves insulin sensitivity, lowers hepatic glucose output and diminishes hyperglycaemic symptoms.
• Sulfonylureas (e.g., glipizide, glyburide, glimepiride) – stimulate pancreatic insulin secretion and reduce symptomatic hyperglycaemia.
• DPP-4 inhibitors (e.g., sitagliptin) and GLP-1 receptor agonists (e.g., liraglutide, semaglutide) – enhance incretin activity, lower glucose and can improve fatigue/polydipsia related to hyperglycaemia.
• SGLT2 inhibitors (e.g., empagliflozin, canagliflozin) – promote renal glucose excretion, decrease blood glucose and improve symptomatic polyuria/polydipsia over time.
• Thiazolidinediones (e.g., pioglitazone) – improve insulin sensitivity and thereby alleviate hyperglycaemia-related symptoms.
The collective evidence and clinical guidelines confirm that these medications are effective in controlling blood glucose levels and, by extension, alleviating the symptoms attributable to uncontrolled diabetes. Hence, the statement that diabetes medications are known to alleviate symptoms of the condition is supported by broad biomedical consensus.
